question: Asked general-knowledge questions, people sometimes gave odds of a million to one that they were right. How often were they?
options: All but once in a thousand
answer: About nine times in ten. In Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein's 1977 experiments, answers backed at odds between 10,000 and a million to one were right only 85 to 90% of the time. The feeling had come loose from the record: wrong about once in eight, where the odds promised once in a million.
move: Score how often your surest answers turn out right, then believe that score.
ask: When I feel 99% sure, how often have I actually turned out right at that level?
trap: Letting the stated million-to-one odds set the expected hit rate.
reference: Fischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein, Knowing with certainty: The appropriateness of extreme confidence, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 3 (4), 1977, pp. 552-564
